summary.text: Lucas congruences pair the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\), whose signs oppose while their relevant binomial products agree, proving vanishing for indices \(p,\ldots,2p-2\); at index \(p-1\), the boundary values are \(1\) and \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), the latter because all but the central summand vanish modulo \(p\). The resulting Hankel matrices are anti-triangular, so their determinants are the reversal-permutation sign \((-1)^{\binom p2}\) times the \(p\)-th power of the anti-diagonal value, yielding the two claimed residues.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
             \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and perform all calculations below in the field
\(\mathbb F_p\), unless otherwise indicated.

We first record the binomial congruences that will be used.

### 1. Binomial congruences modulo \(p\)

Lucas's congruence in the two-digit form says that
\[
 \binom nk\equiv
 \binom{n\bmod p}{k\bmod p}
 \binom{\lfloor n/p\rfloor}{\lfloor k/p\rfloor}\pmod p.
 \tag{1}
\]
For the ranges needed below, neither \(n\) nor \(k\) has more than two base-\(p\) digits. This form of Lucas's congruence follows, for example, by comparing coefficients in
\[
(1+X)^n=(1+X)^{n\bmod p}\bigl((1+X)^p\bigr)^{\lfloor n/p\rfloor}
 \equiv (1+X)^{n\bmod p}(1+X^p)^{\lfloor n/p\rfloor}
 \pmod p.
\]

In particular, if \(0\le m<p\) and \(0\le k<2p\), then
\[
 \binom{p+m}{k}\equiv \binom m{k\bmod p}.
 \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, the upper base-\(p\) digits are \((m,1)\), while
\(\lfloor k/p\rfloor\) is either \(0\) or \(1\), so the second Lucas factor is always \(\binom10=\binom11=1\).

We will also use
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\qquad(0\le k\le p-1).
 \tag{3}
\]
This follows directly from
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k}
 =\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
 \equiv\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k.
\]

We next need several facts about central binomial coefficients. If \(0\le r<p\) and \(p\le 2r\), then
\[
 \binom{2r}{r}\equiv0.
 \tag{4}
\]
To see this using (1), note that the low base-\(p\) digit of \(2r\) is \(2r-p\), which is strictly smaller than \(r\). Thus the low-digit Lucas factor is
\(\binom{2r-p}{r}=0\).

For the shifted central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}\), where \(0\le r<p\), there are two cases. If \(2r<p\), then the base-\(p\) digits of \(2(p+r)\) are \((2r,2)\), while those of \(p+r\) are \((r,1)\). Hence
\[
 \binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}
 \equiv \binom{2r}{r}\binom21
 =2\binom{2r}{r}.
 \tag{5}
\]
If \(p\le2r\), the low digit of the upper argument is \(2r-p<r\), and consequently
\[
 \binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}\equiv0.
 \tag{6}
\]

It follows from (4)--(6) that for all \(0\le j,r<p\),
\[
 \binom{2j}{j}\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}
 \equiv
 \binom{2(p+j)}{p+j}\binom{2r}{r}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, if \(2j<p\) and \(2r<p\), both sides are
\(2\binom{2j}{j}\binom{2r}{r}\). If \(2j<p\le2r\), both sides vanish because the two factors involving \(r\) vanish. Finally, if \(p\le2j\), both sides vanish because the two factors involving \(j\) vanish. These cases exhaust all possibilities.

### 2. The values of \(a(n)\) from \(p-1\) through \(2p-2\)

First consider \(n=p-1\). By (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, this alternating sum of \(p\) terms is \(1\). Therefore
\[
 a(p-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
 \tag{8}
\]

We now show that
\[
 a(p+m)\equiv0\pmod p
 \qquad(0\le m\le p-2).
 \tag{9}
\]
Because \(p+m<2p\), congruence (2) gives
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom m{k\bmod p}
\qquad(0\le k\le p+m).
\]
Split the defining sum for \(a(p+m)\) into the terms with \(0\le k<p\) and those with \(k=p+j\), \(0\le j\le m\). In the first part, the terms with \(k>m\) vanish because \(\binom mk=0\). Thus the first part is
\[
 S=\sum_{j=0}^m(-1)^j\binom mj^4.
\]
The second part is
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^m(-1)^{p+j}\binom mj^4=-S,
\]
because \(p\) is odd. Hence the two parts cancel, proving (9).

### 3. The corresponding values of \(c(n)\)

We first prove
\[
 c(p+m)\equiv0\pmod p
 \qquad(0\le m\le p-2).
 \tag{10}
\]
Again split the defining sum at \(p\). By (2),
\[
 \binom{p+m}{k}^2\equiv \binom m{k\bmod p}^2.
\]
In the part \(0\le k<p\), all terms with \(k>m\) vanish. Write the remaining index as \(j\), where \(0\le j\le m\), and put
\[
 r=m-j.
\]
Then \(0\le r<p\). The term indexed by \(j\) is
\[
 T_j=(-1)^j\binom mj^2
      \binom{2j}{j}\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}.
 \tag{11}
\]
The corresponding term in the second part, indexed by \(p+j\), is
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_j
&=(-1)^{p+j}\binom mj^2
  \binom{2(p+j)}{p+j}
  \binom{2r}{r}\\
&=-(-1)^j\binom mj^2
  \binom{2(p+j)}{p+j}
  \binom{2r}{r},
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
where we used that \(p\) is odd and that
\(p+m-(p+j)=m-j=r\). By the central-binomial identity (7), the unsigned products in (11) and (12) are equal. Therefore \(T_j+U_j=0\) for every \(j\), and summing over \(0\le j\le m\) proves (10).

It remains to calculate \(c(p-1)\). Set
\[
 t=\frac{p-1}{2},
\]
so that \(p=2t+1\) and \(2t=p-1\). We claim that in the sum defining \(c(p-1)\), every term except the one with \(k=t\) vanishes modulo \(p\).

If \(k<t\), then
\[
 r=p-1-k>t,
\]
so \(r<p\) and \(2r\ge p\). By (4),
\(\binom{2r}{r}\equiv0\), which kills the term. If \(k>t\), then \(k<p\) and \(2k\ge p\), so (4) gives
\(\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0\). Thus only \(k=t\) survives.

At \(k=t\), both central binomial factors are
\[
 \binom{2t}{t}=\binom{p-1}{t}\equiv(-1)^t

after applying (3), and the squared binomial factor is also
\(\binom{p-1}{t}^2\equiv((-1)^t)^2\). Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
c(p-1)
&\equiv (-1)^t
 \bigl((-1)^t\bigr)^2
 \bigl((-1)^t\bigr)
 \bigl((-1)^t\bigr)\\
&=(-1)^{5t}=(-1)^t.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
 c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
 \tag{13}
\]

### 4. An anti-triangular Hankel determinant

We use the following elementary determinant fact. Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, let \(d\ge0\), and let \(s(0),s(1),\ldots,s(2d)\in R\) satisfy
\[
 s(d)=v,
 \qquad
 s(x)=0\quad(d<x\le2d).
\]
Then
\[
 \det\bigl(s(i+j)\bigr)_{0\le i,j\le d}
 =(-1)^{\binom{d+1}{2}}v^{d+1}.
 \tag{14}
\]

Here is a direct proof. In the determinant expansion, a permutation \(\sigma\) can contribute a nonzero term only if
\(i+\sigma(i)\le d\) for every \(i\), because all entries strictly beyond the anti-diagonal vanish. But
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^d(i+\sigma(i))
 =2\sum_{i=0}^d i=d(d+1),
\]
which is also the sum of \(d+1\) copies of \(d\). Hence if every
\(i+\sigma(i)\le d\), equality of the sums forces
\(i+\sigma(i)=d\) for every \(i\). Thus the only potentially nonzero permutation is the reversal
\(\sigma(i)=d-i\). Its product of matrix entries is \(v^{d+1}\). Every pair of positions is an inversion of the reversal, so its number of inversions is
\(\binom{d+1}{2}\), and its sign is
\((-1)^{\binom{d+1}{2}}\). This proves (14).

Reduction modulo \(p\) commutes with the determinant, since a determinant is an integer polynomial in the matrix entries. We may therefore apply (14) directly over \(\mathbb F_p\).

### 5. The determinant formed from \(a(n)\)

Let
\[
 A=\bigl(a(i+j)\bigr)_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Take \(d=p-1\). The indices strictly beyond the anti-diagonal range from \(p\) to \(2p-2\). By (9), all corresponding values of \(a\) vanish modulo \(p\), while (8) says that the anti-diagonal value is \(a(p-1)=1\). Formula (14) gives
\[
 \det A\equiv(-1)^{\binom p2}\pmod p.
\]
If \(p=2t+1\), where \(t=(p-1)/2\), then
\[
 \binom p2=\frac{p(p-1)}2=(2t+1)t\equiv t\pmod2.
\]
Hence
\[
 (-1)^{\binom p2}=(-1)^t=(-1)^{(p-1)/2},
\]
and therefore
\[
 \boxed{\det\bigl(a(i+j)\bigr)_{0\le i,j<p}
 \equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.}
\]

### 6. The determinant formed from \(c(n)\)

Let
\[
 C=\bigl(c(i+j)\bigr)_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Again put \(d=p-1\). By (10), all entries strictly beyond the anti-diagonal vanish modulo \(p\). By (13), the common anti-diagonal value is
\[
 v=c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^t,
 \qquad t=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
Thus (14) yields
\[
 \det C
 \equiv(-1)^{\binom p2}\bigl((-1)^t\bigr)^p.
\]
We already know that \((-1)^{\binom p2}=(-1)^t\). Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
 \bigl((-1)^t\bigr)^p=(-1)^{tp}=(-1)^t.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \det C\equiv(-1)^t(-1)^t=(-1)^{2t}=1\pmod p.

aThus
\[
 \boxed{\det\bigl(c(i+j)\bigr)_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p.}
\]

Both asserted determinant congruences follow.
